newsitem.title: USA: Weld resigns, vows fight for Mexico envoy post.
newsitem.headline: Weld resigns, vows fight for Mexico envoy post.

text.p: William Weld, President Bill Clinton's choice as ambassador to Mexico, said on Monday he was resigning the governorship of Massachusetts to fight full time to overturn conservative opposition to his nomination.

Weld told a packed State House news conference he was resigning effective at 5 p.m. EDT (2100 GMT) on Tuesday because "I don't believe it would be fair to the people of Massachusetts to permit the conduct of their government to become embroiled in the vagaries of Washington politics."

To those who suggested surrendering the governor's corner office meant Weld gives up a powerful tool with which to fight for his confirmation, the governor said, "First of all, if you know me, you know I don't play the Washington rules. But the more powerful point is that is not something the governor's office should be used for. This office belongs to the people, not to me."

The nomination of Weld, a fiscal conservative and socially liberal Republican, to be U.S. ambassador to Mexico is likely to be blocked by fellow Republican Sen. Jesse Helms of North Carolina, the conservative chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee.

Helms, who has the power to derail the appointment by not scheduling a hearing in his committee, has publicly said he objects to Weld's views on the medicinal use of marijuana and to his drug prosecution record.

Weld, describing himself as an "ordinary citizen of Massachusetts," said he will go to Washington on Thursday to ask "a very simple question, which is, why shouldn't there be a hearing on our country's representation in Mexico and our relationship with Mexico -- one of our most important allies? ... Why shouldn't there be a hearing on this nomination?

"It's very hard to explain why there shouldn't be a hearing, particularly if Senator Helms's objection is, as he says, based on policy differences. Policy differences are what congressional hearings were invented for," Weld said.

Earlier on Tuesday, Marc Thiessen, a spokesman for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said the panel had not seen a "nominee conduct himself this way before." He said: "This is just a PR stunt for the governor, and we wish him luck."
Asked whether Helms would still block Weld's bid, the spokesman asked, "Have we said anything to indicate a change in views?" He declined to comment further.
White House spokesman Joe Lockhart, travelling with Clinton in California, praised Weld's decision.

"Both the White House and the governor have to work on building support for him on Capitol Hill, and I think he (Weld) believed he was in the best position to do that if he resigned and worked on it full time," Lockhart said.
State Department spokesman James Foley told reporters Weld would be coming to Washington later this week and would be briefed by senior department officials.

"We're not under illusions that this is going to be easy but we intend to make the case along with him ... that he's an eminently qualified public servant who could bring a lot of unique abilities to the job in Mexico ...," he said.

A spokesman for Republican Sen. John Chafee of Rhode Island, who supports Weld, said he was circulating a letter among his Senate Republican colleagues to try to develop a "larger cheering section" for Weld.

Meanwhile, Massachusetts Lt. Gov. Paul Cellucci, also a Republican, will assume the governorship on Tuesday. The two share a similar political philosophy and Weld, who called Cellucci his co-governor, expressed strong support for him.
